name: Lepakshi Veerabhadra Temple
summary: A jewel of the Vijayanagara age in Andhra Pradesh, the Veerabhadra temple at Lepakshi is famed for its ceiling of vivid frescoes, a celebrated “hanging pillar,” a giant monolithic Nandi, and an unfinished wedding hall frozen in mid-carving.

sections.history: The temple was built in the sixteenth century, in the great age of the Vijayanagara empire, by the brothers Virupanna and Viranna, officers in the service of the emperor Achyuta Raya. It is dedicated to Veerabhadra, the fierce warrior form of Shiva. Legend and history mingle in its unfinished state: tradition holds that Virupanna was accused of misusing the treasury on the temple and blinded himself in grief, leaving the great Kalyana Mandapa forever incomplete — a story the bare, half-carved pillars seem to confirm.
sections.architecture: Lepakshi is a treasury of Vijayanagara art. Its mandapa ceilings carry some of the finest surviving murals of the period, including a vast painting of Veerabhadra, their mineral colours still glowing. A famous “hanging pillar” rests so lightly that a cloth can be passed beneath it, a feat of balance that has puzzled visitors for centuries. Nearby stands one of India’s largest monolithic Nandis, and within the complex a great Nagalinga — a serpent coiled over a linga — is cut from a single boulder. The unfinished Kalyana Mandapa, its pillars richly begun and abruptly abandoned, is as eloquent as any completed hall.
sections.legends: The very name Lepakshi is tied to the Ramayana: here, it is said, the bird Jatayu fell wounded after trying to stop Ravana from carrying off Sita, and Rama, finding him, said "Le, pakshi" — "rise, bird" — giving the place its name. A great footprint in the stone is revered as Sita’s. The temple’s human story is no less moving: the blinding of its builder Virupanna, and the unfinished hall left as if the chisels had only just been set down, lending Lepakshi a poignancy rare among temples.
sections.festivals: The temple observes the Shaiva festivals, with Maha Shivaratri and the annual kalyanam of the deities kept with worship and processions. Cultural programmes and heritage events increasingly bring visitors to celebrate Lepakshi’s Vijayanagara art among its painted halls. As both a living Veerabhadra shrine and a protected monument, it draws pilgrims and lovers of art alike through the year.
sections.experience: A visit to Lepakshi rewards the eye at every turn. Entering the pillared halls, one looks up to ceilings alive with painted gods and processions; walking on, the guides point out the hanging pillar and the abrupt end of the unfinished mandapa. Outside, the colossal monolithic Nandi gazes toward the Nagalinga on its rock, and the whole complex, set on a low rocky hill called Kurma Saila, catches the warm light of the Rayalaseema plain. Few temples so vividly combine great art, a haunting human story, and living worship.

visit.timings: Generally open from around 6:00 am to 6:00 pm daily; as a protected monument and living temple, worship and visiting hours may vary on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest dress is appreciated, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed at the temple.
visit.photography: Photography of the halls, murals, and monuments is generally allowed; follow any posted rules within the sanctum and during worship.
visit.gettingThere: Lepakshi is in Sri Sathya Sai district, about 15 km from Hindupur and 120 km from Bengaluru, whose airport is the nearest; Hindupur is the closest railway station, and the temple is a short drive from the highway.
